scenes.headline: Dataclasses & Pydantic Models
scenes.subtitle: Structured records without boilerplate
scenes.narration: Both dataclasses and pydantic give you clean, typed record types instead of loose dictionaries, but they solve subtly different problems that are worth telling apart.

scenes.headline: A dataclass
scenes.narration: Applying the dataclass decorator to a class with annotated fields tells Python to auto-generate the boilerplate for you. From these three fields it produces an __init__ constructor, a readable __repr__, and value-based equality, all without a line of manual code. The ts field even shows how to give a default. It's the fastest way to declare a lightweight, typed record.

scenes.headline: A pydantic model
scenes.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Event(BaseModel):
    user_id: int
    action: str
    ts: float = 0.0

e = Event(user_id='42', action='click')  # coerced to int
scenes.narration: A pydantic model looks almost identical, but it does far more at construction time. It validates every incoming field against its declared type and coerces where sensible, so the string forty-two here is accepted and converted to the integer forty-two. If a value truly can't be made to fit, pydantic raises a detailed validation error pinpointing exactly what went wrong.

scenes.headline: dataclass vs pydantic
scenes.narration: A dataclass ships in the standard library with zero dependencies, but it trusts you completely and performs no validation on the data you pass. Pydantic adds real runtime validation and type coercion, which makes it invaluable wherever data crosses an I/O boundary. Use dataclasses for tidy internal structures you already control, and pydantic wherever untrusted external data enters your system.

scenes.headline: When to reach for each
scenes.narration: For internal configuration objects you assemble yourself, a dataclass is the lean, dependency-free choice. For parsing an API response or a JSON payload from outside, pydantic's validation is exactly what you want. Any time correctness of incoming data matters, lean on pydantic. But when you're merely grouping a few related fields for convenience, a dataclass keeps things simple.

scenes.text: Dataclasses give free boilerplate; pydantic adds validation. Validate all external data with pydantic.
scenes.narration: Reach for pydantic at every trust boundary where external data arrives, and use dataclasses for lightweight internal records you already control.
